response:
I've conducted a thorough review of the artifact against all 170+ prior findings. Below are genuinely novel findings — issues not covered or only tangentially touched by prior rounds.

---

FINDING_ID: R6_F001
SEVERITY: 0.85
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION: 0.82
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `DynamicManager.update_fingerprints()` computes `total_classes` from ALL findings in the current round across ALL models, but `obs_c` (coverage) is computed as `len(model_classes) / total_classes`. If model A finds flaw classes {1,2} and model B finds flaw classes {3,4,5}, then `total_classes=5`. Model A gets `C=2/5=0.4`, model B gets `C=3/5=0.6`. But if model B is excluded next round and model A now finds classes {1,2,3}, `total_classes=3` and `C=3/3=1.0`. The coverage metric is not comparable across rounds because the denominator changes with the active model set composition. EMA smoothing over incomparable values produces a meaningless composite. This is distinct from CC2_R1_F007/CC2_R3_F006 which note the denominator is round-local rather than cumulative — this finding identifies that even within a single round, the denominator is pool-composition-dependent, making cross-round EMA invalid.

FINDING_ID: R6_F002
SEVERITY: 0.82
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION: 0.78
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `ConvergenceDetector._novel_classes()` computes round-level equivalence classes independently from cumulative classes, then checks novelty by comparing individual members across the two clusterings. But single-linkage clustering is non-monotone under set union: findings A and B may be in separate round-level classes (sim(A,B) < tau_sim), but when combined with prior finding C in the cumulative set, C bridges them (sim(A,C) >= tau_sim AND sim(B,C) >= tau_sim), merging them into one cumulative class. The novelty check compares round-level class members against cumulative class members, but the round-level class boundaries don't match cumulative class boundaries. A round-level class could be declared "novel" because none of its members match prior findings, yet in the cumulative clustering those same members are absorbed into an existing class via a bridge finding from the same round. This is a structural inconsistency between the two clustering scopes that prior findings (CC2_F009, CC2_R5_F005) noted superficially but did not trace to the single-linkage bridging mechanism.

FINDING_ID: R6_F003
SEVERITY: 0.79
FLAW_CLASS: 4
ABSTRACTION: 0.85
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: The `DynamicManager` has no mechanism to distinguish between "model was allocated work and returned nothing" vs "model was not allocated work this round." `process_round()` iterates `responses.items()` and calls `detect_failure()` only for models that appear in the responses dict. A model that was allocated tasks but simply didn't respond (network partition, crash) produces no response entry, so no failure is detected, no `record_failure(model_id, True)` is called, and the model's failure history records nothing. Meanwhile, `record_failure(model_id, False)` is also never called for that model, so its failure rate denominator doesn't grow. This is distinct from ChatGPT_ROUND2_F004 ("missing responses treated as success-by-omission") and Codex_F014 ("allocation is always None") — this finding identifies that the failure history statistics themselves become biased: a model that intermittently drops responses has an artificially low failure rate because non-responses don't increment either counter.

FINDING_ID: R6_F004
SEVERITY: 0.77
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION: 0.72
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `DiminishingReturnsDetector.marginal_value()` returns `float("inf")` when `c_r <= epsilon_cost` and `delta_y > 0`. This infinite value propagates into `smoothed_marginal_value()` via `np.mean(values)`, but the method filters with `math.isfinite(mv)`, discarding infinite values. So a free round (cost=0) with positive yield is simply ignored in the smoothing window. If the first round is free (common for BLIND rounds where no API cost is incurred), `smoothed_marginal_value(0)` returns `0.0` (empty values list after filtering), and `stop(0)` would return `True` if `r_min` weren't guarding it. More critically, if a later round happens to be free (e.g., cached responses), its positive yield is silently dropped from the smoothing average, potentially making the smoothed value appear lower than it should be and triggering premature stopping.

FINDING_ID: R6_F005
SEVERITY: 0.75
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION: 0.68
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `RoleAssignment.reassign()` computes `pool_max` from active models only, then uses it for `_capability_score()` which calls `as_normalised_array(pool_max)`. The normalisation divides each dimension by `pool_max` and inverts D_decay. But `_capability_score` is called with `Role.COL` only — it never recomputes PM or PAR scores. The `capability_scores` dict (used by `get_ordering()`) retains the original scores from `assign()`, computed with the original full-pool `pool_max`. After reassignment, `get_ordering(Role.COL)` returns stale scores while the actual COL selection used different scores. This is noted by ChatGPT_R3_F009 but the deeper issue is that the COL hysteresis comparison (`col_scores[best_col_id] <= col_scores[current_col] + epsilon_rho`) uses scores computed with the active-only `pool_max`, while the initial COL was selected with the full-pool `pool_max`. These scores are on different scales — the hysteresis band `epsilon_rho=0.05` may be too tight or too loose depending on how much `pool_max` shifted.

FINDING_ID: R6_F006
SEVERITY: 0.73
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION: 0.65
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `CorrelatedFailureModel.set_vulnerability()` uses `frozenset({model_i, model_j})` as the key. When `model_i == model_j`, the frozenset has only one element, so `set_vulnerability("m1", "m1", 0.5)` stores `frozenset({"m1"}): 0.5`. But `get_vulnerability("m1", "m1")` has an early return `if model_i == model_j: return 1.0` that never consults the dict. So self-vulnerability can be set but never read, and the stored value silently diverges from the returned value. This is partially noted by ChatGPT_ROUND4_F012 ("permits self-vulnerability entries") but that finding doesn't identify the read-write inconsistency: the write succeeds, the read ignores it, and no error is raised.

FINDING_ID: R6_F007
SEVERITY: 0.71
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION: 0.70
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer._solve_greedy()` assigns tasks in criticality-descending order, giving high-criticality tasks first pick of models. But `_redundancy_target()` for high-criticality tasks returns `K` (all models). When PM is excluded (K>1), the greedy loop assigns to `K-1` admissible models, consuming their capacity. Lower-criticality tasks then find all models partially loaded. The greedy order creates a systematic bias: high-criticality tasks get optimal placement while low-criticality tasks get residual capacity. This is the opposite of what a balanced allocation should do — the objective function `J(A)` penalises variance, but the greedy solver never backtracks to rebalance after high-criticality assignments consume disproportionate capacity. Prior findings (CC2_R3_F013, CC2_R4_F010, CC2_R5_F010) note the redundancy/admissibility mismatch but not this systematic load-imbalance bias from the greedy ordering.

FINDING_ID: R6_F008
SEVERITY: 0.69
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION: 0.60
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `DynamicManager.__init__()` initialises `_round_metrics` with keys from `self.models`, but `update_fingerprints()` iterates over `self.failure_handler.active_models` and appends to `self._round_metrics[model_id]`. If a model was never in the original pool (impossible currently, but if `active_models` is externally mutated — which is possible since `FailureHandler._active_models` is a regular set), `_round_metrics[model_id]` raises `KeyError`. More practically: if a model is excluded and later the set is inspected, `_round_metrics` retains entries for excluded models with incomplete round histories (missing entries for rounds after exclusion), while active models have complete histories. Any analysis assuming uniform-length metric histories across models will produce index errors or misaligned comparisons.

FINDING_ID: R6_F009
SEVERITY: 0.68
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION: 0.74
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: The `kappa` combined metric uses `min(kappa_set, max(0, kappa_rate), kappa_adopt)`. The `max(0, kappa_rate)` clamp means that when `kappa_rate` is negative (finding rate increasing — degradation), it contributes `0` to the min. But `kappa_set` and `kappa_adopt` could both be high (e.g., 0.95). The combined `kappa = min(0.95, 0, 0.95) = 0`, which correctly blocks convergence. However, if `kappa_rate` is exactly 0 (rate unchanged from round 1), `kappa = min(kappa_set, 0, kappa_adopt) = 0`, which also blocks convergence even though a stable rate is not evidence against convergence — it's evidence of a steady state. The metric conflates "rate increasing" (bad) with "rate unchanged" (neutral) by clamping both to 0. Prior finding CC2_R4_F017 notes that any single metric can block convergence but doesn't identify this specific conflation at the zero boundary.

FINDING_ID: R6_F010
SEVERITY: 0.66
FLAW_CLASS: 3
ABSTRACTION: 0.55
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: The `FailureHandler.get_recovery()` policy for `FailureType.FORMAT` returns `DEGRADE` on first occurrence and `RETRY_CLARIFIED` on repetition. This is inverted relative to standard escalation patterns (noted by Gemini_REVIEW_F004, CC2_R2_F010, CC2_R3_F016). But the deeper issue not captured by those findings is that `DEGRADE` is never actually executed anywhere — `process_round()` only checks for `ABORT`, and `FailureHandler` only executes `EXCLUDE`. So the first FORMAT failure returns `DEGRADE` which is silently ignored, and the repeated FORMAT failure returns `RETRY_CLARIFIED` which is also silently ignored. The net effect is that FORMAT failures have no operational consequence regardless of repetition count — they are functionally equivalent to `LOG_ONLY`.

FINDING_ID: R6_F011
SEVERITY: 0.64
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION: 0.58
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `update_fingerprints()` computes `obs["D_decay"]` as the fraction of a model's findings that are similar to ANY prior finding from ANY model. This means if model A produces a finding similar to model B's prior finding, model A's D_decay increases. But D_decay is supposed to measure detection decay — how much a model repeats itself, not how much it agrees with other models. Cross-model agreement is actually a positive signal (corroboration), not decay. The metric penalises models for independently discovering the same flaw, which is the opposite of the intended semantics. Prior finding CC2_F022 notes the semantic mismatch between "duplication rate" and "detection decay rate" but frames it as a naming issue. This finding identifies that the cross-model comparison makes the metric actively counterproductive: it punishes the exact behaviour (independent corroboration) that the framework is designed to reward.

FINDING_ID: R6_F012
SEVERITY: 0.62
FLAW_CLASS: 4
ABSTRACTION: 0.80
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: The `DynamicManager` creates a new `LoadBalancer` instance on every `get_allocation()` call, passing `self.role_assignment.role_map`. But `role_map` may contain entries for models that are no longer active (excluded via `FailureHandler`). `get_live_models()` correctly filters to active models, so the `LoadBalancer.models` list is correct. However, `_admissibility_mask()` computes `k_total = sum(1 for r in self.role_map.values() if r in (Role.COL, Role.PAR, Role.PM))` — this counts ALL entries in `role_map`, including excluded models. If `k_total > 1` (which it almost always is since `role_map` retains excluded models), PM is excluded from tasks. But if only PM survives, `k_total` from the stale `role_map` is still > 1, so PM is excluded from all tasks, and the admissibility mask is all zeros. The fallback `admissible = list(range(K))` catches this, but it means the PM-only degraded mode always triggers the fallback path rather than the intended `k_total == 1` path. This is related to Codex_F011 but that finding focuses on the stale `role_map` causing F3 violations; this finding identifies that the `k_total` computation from the stale map systematically prevents the K=1 degraded-mode path from ever activating.

FINDING_ID: R6_F013
SEVERITY: 0.60
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION: 0.52
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `ManagerEventStream.emit()` appends to `_buffer` and `_all_events` before calling `_callback`. If the callback calls `drain()`, it gets the event that triggered the callback (since it's already in `_buffer`). But if the callback calls `emit()` recursively (e.g., a callback that emits a derived event), the recursive `emit()` appends to `_buffer` and `_all_events`, then calls `_callback` again, creating unbounded recursion. There is no re-entrancy guard. A callback that conditionally emits events (e.g., "on TIMEOUT, emit RETRY") will stack-overflow. This is distinct from ChatGPT_ROUND2_F007 (exception safety) and CC2_R3_F005 (callback exception after append) — this is about recursive re-entrancy causing infinite recursion.

FINDING_ID: R6_F014
SEVERITY: 0.58
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION: 0.48
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `Allocation.model_load()` builds `task_map = {t.task_id: t for t in tasks}` on every call, then looks up tasks by ID. But the `tasks` parameter is caller-supplied and may not match `self.task_ids`. If the caller passes a different task list (e.g., tasks from a different round, or a subset), `task_map[tid]` raises `KeyError` for any `tid` in `self.task_ids` not present in the supplied `tasks`. There is no validation that the supplied tasks cover all allocated task IDs. Similarly, `model_load_fraction()` calls `model_load()` with the same vulnerability. This is distinct from CC2_R3_F009 which notes the `task_map` rebuild pattern but focuses on the `model_ids.index()` call.

FINDING_ID: R6_F015
SEVERITY: 0.55
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION: 0.65
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `ConvergenceDetector.estimate_gamma()` computes the Duane parameter as `log(round_idx) / (log(cum_r) - log(cum_1))`. When `round_idx=2`, `cum_r = |F^(<=2)|`, `cum_1 = |F^(<=1)|`. If `cum_r = cum_1` (no new classes in round 2), the method returns `float("inf")`. But `float("inf")` as a gamma estimate is semantically wrong — it should indicate perfect convergence (no new failures), but the Duane model interprets gamma > 1 as reliability growth and gamma → ∞ as instantaneous convergence. The method returns `0.0` when `cum_r < cum_1`, which is impossible (cumulative classes can only grow or stay equal). The `cum_r <= cum_1` guard conflates two cases: `cum_r == cum_1` (convergence) and `cum_r < cum_1` (impossible). The impossible case should be an error, not a silent `0.0`.

FINDING_ID: R6_F016
SEVERITY: 0.52
FLAW_CLASS: 6
ABSTRACTION: 0.45
VERIFIED: FALSE
DESCRIPTION: `RoundProgressionFSM.__post_init__()` sets `current_round = 0` (BLIND = round 0). But `current_round` is declared with `field(init=False, default=-1)` in the dataclass definition. The `__post_init__` override sets it to 0, so the default of -1 is never observable. However, if someone subclasses or copies the pattern and relies on the declared default, they get -1 instead of 0. More concretely: `current_round` is typed as `int` but semantically represents a round index that should be non-negative during normal operation. The transition from BLIND to SYNTH does NOT update `current_round` (it stays 0), and the transition from SYNTH to ROUND_1 sets it to 1. So during the SYNTH state, `current_round = 0`, which is the same as during BLIND. This is the core of Codex_F001, but the additional issue here is that the dataclass declaration with `default=-1` is misleading documentation — it suggests -1 is a valid sentinel value, but no code path ever checks for or handles -1.
